title: People between the field book and the machine

blocks.text: A calculation still passed through several hands. Survey staff made and recorded the observations; someone prepared the cards; programmers and operators ran the job; the results came back as tables or tape for technical staff to inspect. If a coordinate looked wrong, it had to be traced through the output, the input deck and the original field record.

blocks.text: That division could separate knowledge of the machine from knowledge of the place. A programmer could produce a clean run from bad observations; a surveyor could spot an implausible position but need help changing the input. Reliable work depended on both kinds of expertise meeting at the same job.

blocks.text: The practical lesson has lasted: retain identifiers and source observations, document the calculation, and check outputs against independent control. Electronic processing made it easier to repeat a method; it did not make a result self-validating.
